source.title: Building on Efficient Foundations: Effectively Training LLMs with Structured Feedforward Layers
source.authors: Xiuying Wei; Skander Moalla; Razvan Pascanu; Caglar Gulcehre

record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out language-model loss across model sizes and training compute, using structured FFNs rather than the original dense-model setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-compute scaling curves with linear fits for illustration and tests downstream scores across model sizes. It does not validate predictions fitted on small runs or sweep parameter/token allocations to find a compute-optimal split. The use of 20 tokens per baseline parameter follows a cited scaling-law setup; it is not an optimal-allocation result from this study.
record.test_reason: It reports held-out loss for dense and structured-FFN LMs at four Chinchilla-allocated sizes (about 2 orders of compute), with fitted scaling lines. It also reports zero-shot task scores across sizes. This is a new architectural setting, not a replication of the original method. The scaling law is mainly used as a tool (20 tokens per parameter), so the test is weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that all structured FFNs show steeper training-FLOPs scaling curves than dense models. They also find that wide-and-structured networks reach equal or lower perplexity with fewer parameters at equal FLOPs, and scale favourably in the overtraining regime. Self-guided training narrows the perplexity gap. They state they did not explore optimal scaling laws for structured matrices, and that the structured curves are not at their compute-optimal trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares dense Transformers with LowRank, BlockDense, and BlockShuffle FFN parameterizations, rather than reproducing the original dense-model scaling procedure. It uses a chosen token allocation and does not fit or validate an optimal compute-allocation law.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling behavior varies with FFN parameterization; the structured curves are described as steeper than the dense curve. The paper also notes that BlockDense and BlockShuffle were explored over limited hyperparameter settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss-vs-training-FLOPs curves are steeper for structured FFNs (LowRank, BlockDense, BlockShuffle) than for dense Transformers. The gap to dense shrinks with size, e.g. LowRank-32% goes from 0.12 at s to 0.08 at xl.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-scaling slope of LM loss depends on the FFN parameterization (architecture family), not only on parameter count.

record.problems: The checklist states that the results are single training runs without error bars because of compute cost. The study covers models up to 1.3B, uses one main language-modeling dataset, reports limited configurations for some structures, and explicitly does not investigate optimal scaling laws for structured matrices.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining Table 6 structured-FFN scaling points across Transformer-s, -m, and -l for BlockDense and BlockShuffle were omitted to stay within the 60-row limit; the retained rows cover dense and LowRank results across all four sizes and BlockDense/BlockShuffle at Transformer-xl. Table 8 RefinedWeb validation perplexity was omitted because it is not a downstream-task score. No separate LAMBADA perplexity rows were added because Table 8 reports LAMBADA as a paired accuracy/perplexity value.

untested.parts: Scaling over several orders of magnitude: the compute span is about 124x and parameters span 110M-1.3B. Separate parameter-only and token-only laws are not tested. No goodness of fit or exponents are reported; the linear fits are 'for better illustration'.
No small-run fit is validated against much larger runs.
There is no compute-optimal sweep. Structured models are explicitly not at their optimal trade-off.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not varied.
The CIFAR-10 experiments are not scaling studies. Repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer scaling are not tested.
There are only three sizes. No fit of downstream scores against scale or loss is made, and nothing is predicted.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule and data choices are not compared.

missing.what: RefinedWeb validation perplexity vs model size for dense and wide-and-structured models trained on 300B tokens (dense 16.02→12.34→10.76). This is loss scaling in the overtraining regime, relevant to V1.
BlockDense and BlockShuffle s/m/l loss points, needed to read those series' trends. They are declared left out but are needed for R13-R16 to bear on V1.
Winogrande scores and a possible fourth (xl) size appear only in Fig. 5. The text says four dense sizes were trained on 300B tokens, but Table 8 lists three.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. Its scaling evidence is four points per series, from single runs without error bars; the linear fits are illustrative. The reader's V1 limits_scope label was removed because it described untested range, not a failure; that range is now listed as untested. The tranche was changed from T2 to T3, since the paper places Chinchilla-style loss scaling in a new structured-FFN setting rather than taking a new method to the same question.

versions.untested_parts: It tests loss scaling with training FLOPs over four model sizes for selected Transformer and structured-FFN configurations. It does not independently sweep parameters, tokens, and compute while holding the other two non-bottleneck, and does not establish scaling over several orders of magnitude in parameter count.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep identifies loss-minimising parameter and token counts or their growth with compute.
The study changes FFN parameterization and some attention configurations; it does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
The CIFAR-10 experiments are not modality-specific scaling-law tests. The paper does not test the claimed power-law form in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
It reports downstream scores at three model sizes for selected tasks, but does not fit or validate predictions of downstream performance from pretraining loss.

The paper does not compare fitting choices or report fitted exponents and compute-optimal splits across setups. Its structured-model curves being steeper than dense-model curves is not a test of the version's stated fitting-choice and split claims.

relationships.condition: Dense Transformers (Chinchilla 20 tokens/param) and LowRank-FFN variants on RefinedWeb, 1.2e18-2.1e20 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Validation loss falls steadily with compute in each series, and the paper draws fitted scaling lines through the points (R01-R12). No fit quality is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased steadily with compute in every series, with fitted scaling lines through the observations.

relationships.condition: Dense and wide-and-structured models at three sizes trained on 300B tokens; ARC-c/e, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, PIQA zero-shot
relationships.reason: Every task score rises monotonically with model size in both architecture groups (e.g. dense ARC-e 44.65→50.80→58.71). It is only three points, with no predictive fit (R17-R46).
relationships.display_finding: Every task improved at each size increase in both architectures, including dense ARC-e scores of 44.65, 50.80, and 58.71.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
